title: Wrenk and the Sunstone Quest
markdown:
Wrenk’s workshop smelled of singed wire and optimism. Gears lived in piles that had once been systems. The frost-bitten peaks stood outside the shutters like a row of unimpressed relatives, observatories perched on them the way owls perch on opinions. Wrenk was a goblin of the tinkering variety: bright eyes, quicker fingers, a mind that ran ahead of his height. He wanted the sort of nod the elder goblins got, the sort the mountain dwarves collected without asking. What he had instead was a dull grey stone and a polishing cloth he was wearing to threads.

“A little more shine,” he told it. “Then they will see.”

Moss, his ferret, understood the sentence as a cry for help and said so with his nose. Moss was loyalty at the speed of a thrown glove.

The paste had been an accident, as Wrenk’s best ideas usually were: fermented cloudberries, a jar with the wrong label, a dab meant for a hinge. The stone did not merely shine. It woke. Warm amber light filled the workshop like a held breath. It pulsed. Wrenk’s jaw forgot its job. This was the Sunstone of Solara, the mountain’s own argument for endurance, the thing the council of elders were supposed to be guarding in the Spire. A goblin who lost his spectacles three times before breakfast had just given it a second dawn.

“Moss,” Wrenk said, in a voice borrowed from a field mouse, “we have a situation.”

Moss’s look was an entire lecture. Wrenk tried a pouch, a pot, a heap of springs. The stone declined to be modest. He wrapped it in a grimy handkerchief, shoved it into his satchel, and announced a march of military purity: to the Elder’s Spire, straight, no detours, no questions. Moss chirped as if that were a battle plan and not a wish.

The mule track disagreed. It had been designed by goats with better balance and a weaker sense of humour. Wind found the holes in Wrenk’s tunic and moved in. Each switchback offered a new view of how far a goblin could fall if he started believing his own puffery. He pictured the elders laughing, beards shaking, a tinkerer arriving with the heart of the mountain in a dirty cloth. He pictured, worse, arriving and finding they had not noticed the stone was gone. The mist produced Elara instead: tall, moonlight hair, the sort of eyes that had already finished listening. She was the foothills’ famous avalanche-ear, the elf who heard snow consider its options.

“The mountain says you are bound for the Spire,” she said. “I can guide you. I hear the snow speak.”

Wrenk tried gruff. It cracked. “And if I do not wish it?”

Elara’s smile was mild and inconvenient. “Then you may find yourself inside a sudden song of ice and stone.”

He did not send her away. Moss, traitorously sensible, approved.

The first test was a ledge that had given up being a path. A gap opened on a drop that did not bother with details. Wrenk declared it no problem and then discovered that declaring things did not shorten distances. Moss went first, a brown streak, and came back chittering as if the air were a floor. Wrenk jumped because the alternative was remaining a statue. The wind tried to keep him. It failed by a goblin-width.

Around the next bend, theatre had broken out. Zephyr Quickspell, wiry and permanently startled, wore a hat that insulted several laws of balance. Ignis Flameheart stood opposite him in robes that crackled as if they had opinions about weather. They were not duelling so much as marking each other’s homework. Zephyr awarded a plume of fire an eight for flair. Ignis answered with a gust that sent the hat travelling and scored the chaos a seven.

“What in the name of glittering fungi,” Wrenk whispered.

“They think the Sunstone’s return requires a spectacle,” Elara said. “They are competing for the privilege of presenting it.”

Wrenk looked at his own grease-coloured cuffs. He did not own style points. He barely owned paired socks. Zephyr’s quill appeared to be a sliver of lightning, which felt unfair on a mountain that already had weather. Ignis’s hair stood out from her head as if it were taking notes. They scored another pair of spells while Wrenk stood there holding, in a satchel, the object their entire performance was auditioning for. Moss sneezed. It was the most honest sound on the ledge.

Later, on a slope of scree that shifted like a bad mood, the mountain made a sound Wrenk felt in his teeth. Elara stopped as if someone had pulled a string. “Down. Now.” The overhang took them. The avalanche took the place they had been standing, a roaring argument of ice and stone that left the air tasting of cold iron. Elara’s gift was not a parlour trick. It was the difference between a story and a silence.

The spellcasters, less impressed by geology, had seen the glow leak from Wrenk’s satchel. Ignis named the stone hers with a brightness that was not reverence. Zephyr promised artistic magic of a reclaiming sort. Wind and sparks arrived together, a pretty way to steal. Wrenk tripped over the fact of his own feet. The Sunstone rolled for the edge of a drop that did not forgive. Moss became a decision: a yelp, a streak, teeth and paws closing on warmth a breath before the abyss. Elara flicked a sheet of calm air through the worst of the attack. Wrenk scooped ferret and stone and followed her into a maze of outcrops while frustrated glitter stained the snow behind them.

Pride makes a good compass if you enjoy walking in circles. Zephyr and Ignis came on, robes tearing, trails of smoke like garish handwriting. The Spire was close enough to matter. Wrenk felt the stone’s light dip with his courage. He was still the overlooked cog, only now the machine was a mountain.

Then he stumbled, because of course he did. The handkerchief failed. The Sunstone slipped, not toward a polite little hollow, but into a crevasse that opened like a mouth that had been waiting. The clatter that followed was small and final.

Wrenk sat. Wind found his ears. The speech he had been rehearsing for the elders went to frost and dropped off him. He had wanted to be seen. He had been seen, briefly, by two people who wanted the stone for the applause it would buy, and then the mountain had taken the applause and the stone together. Moss pushed at his glove. Elara sat without offering a better version of him. Below, the crevasse made the small sounds of a deep place: melt, grit, an echo that did not care who was listening.

“Sometimes,” she said, no louder than snow, “the journey puts you where you did not mean to stand. What looks lost may only be waiting for a different kind of looking.”

He stared at the dark. He looked at Moss, who had already saved the stone once and was prepared, idiotically, to try again. He looked at Elara, who had heard the mountain in time. The Sunstone was not a ticket to being announced. It was a reason to build something that worked.

“Moss,” he said, and the old workshop tone came back in pieces. “We need a contraption.”

Twine. Pulleys he carried because a goblin who trusts ledges is a goblin who learns once. A grappling hook with more hope than dignity. Moss nosed the hook into a crevice that looked promising if you were a ferret. Elara watched the weather the way other people watch doors. The twine complained. Wrenk cranked anyway.

The elders arrived out of mist as the hook caught, a procession of stern faces with older humour underneath. Elara had signalled; they had come. Behind them, stained and sparking, Zephyr and Ignis arrived too, ambition still wearing yesterday’s theatre.

Wrenk heaved. Moss came up with the Sunstone held as if it were a living coal and equally unwilling to be dropped. The light found Wrenk’s face and, for a moment, made it look like a decision.

“I am Wrenk,” he said, and the air was cold enough to carry it. “The Sunstone belongs with the elders.”

The spellcasters began a protest that had too many adjectives. Grimbark, eldest, beard like a silver fall, lifted one hand and the adjectives died. He looked at the goblin, then at the stone.

“Resourcefulness,” he said. “Loyalty. The light was not put out by greed.” He glanced at the ruined finery behind him. “As for style points, perhaps the lower valleys still applaud amateur theatrics. The mountains prefer substance.”

Night came without a parade. Moonlight found the village roofs and turned them into a second, quieter snow. Wrenk sat on an outcrop with Elara and Moss and watched the windows below behave like fallen stars. The Sunstone was home. Nobody had composed a hymn. What he had instead was a ferret against his wrist, an elf who did not need him to be taller, and the knowledge that a small tinkerer could finish an improbable job and still be, in the morning, himself.
characters: Wrenk (goblin tinkerer who polishes overlooked stones), Moss (a ferret of astonishing speed), Elara (an elf guide who hears avalanches before they begin)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for teens
